extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, journal editors, and mathematics-society leadership (e.g., AMS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on how mathematical journals should operate (editorial structure, peer review, publication workflow, community relations, and open-access practices) and concrete suggestions for improvements. Also practical advice for authors/readers on boycotting paywalled publishers and promoting free access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing / stop wasting paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop wasting paper and fully move to electronic publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates fully digital publication as a basic step; print volumes are obsolete and create unnecessary limits and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: No page/article limits; publish as many good papers as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not limit numbers of papers or pages. Rather, aim for as many good papers as you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the digital age, physical page limits are anachronistic; journals should expand acceptance capacity to serve community needs rather than artificially restrict output to preserve prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve editorial system transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve your electronic editorial system to make it more transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be able to see complete logs of communications, anonymized referee actions, and dates (modelled after APS/PRE systems). Transparency reduces anxiety and increases accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based editorial workflow and queue redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Help editors work as a team, and incentivize them financially. Pay for 20% employment to experts across the world to help you run the journal. The editors work as a team, jointly handling all incoming email and submission/resubmission traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize editors so routine tasks are handled by whoever is available, while substantive decisions remain with assigned Associate Editors; redistribute workloads if someone is backlogged to avoid delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create appeals procedure / editorial board of appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an appeals procedure and add a new type of senior editors who would take the job seriously. The 'Editorial Board' is really a board of appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When papers are rejected, authors should have a formal right to appeal; appeals should be read and signed by a board member who reviews referees' reports and provides a written decision. This serves as a check on associate editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute awards for articles and referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute a number of awards: for best long, short and survey articles in your journal, and for best referees. Outstanding referee award exists at APS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards recognize and incentivize excellence in writing and reviewing; use nominations from editors and discuss at editorial meetings; can be used for career validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and solicit survey/expository articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up new math journals fully dedicated to survey articles, both solicited and contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide budgets and incentives (example: APS pays $1,500/$750 for Reviews of Modern Physics articles) to attract high-quality expository work, since surveys are undervalued but important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize good style; avoid desk rejections for formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to the style, so it’s important to make an effort to avoid being rejected by a non-expert just because of that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should help authors improve presentation; journals that enforce style rigidly at submission can cause unnecessary desk rejections by non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable desk-rejection policy and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: At PRE, about 15-20% of all papers are rejected within days after the initial screening by managing or associate editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use desk rejections to save referee resources, but keep percentages reasonable and avoid opaque or arbitrary screening that wastes authors' time; compare across fields to calibrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast, defined referee turnaround times
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewers are given only three weeks to write the report, but that time can be extended upon request. Typically, editors aim to finish the first round in three months, so the paper can be published in under six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear short deadlines for referees (e.g., 3 weeks) with limited extensions; monitor and be embarrassed by long delays beyond six months to incentivize timely review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for low backlog and fast production turnaround
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paper is accepted at PRE... it gets published online with a unique identifier, usually within 2-3 weeks from the date of acceptance. There is zero backlog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outsource production effectively and ensure quick proof rounds; prioritize online publication speed rather than print scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign referees aiming for two reports; be realistic about referee recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate editors... send it to referees with the goal of obtaining two reports. Asking 4-8 potential referees is normal, but on rare occasions the numbers can be as high as 10-20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should expect to invite multiple potential referees and track recruitment carefully; set norms for number of invites per paper to manage timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial visibility across related journals / transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial system allows editors from one journal see all actions and reports in all other APS journals. If the rejected PRL paper fits the scope of PRE and there are reports suggesting PRE might be suitable, PRE editors try to invite such papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable cross-journal visibility and transfers to speed placement and reduce duplicate review effort; consider mechanisms to invite suitable rejects into sister journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate editor structure: mix of professional and academic editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the editorial work is done by an assortment of Associate Editors, some of whom are employed full time by the APS (all of them physics PhD's), and some are faculty... Such Associate Editors receive a 2 year renewable contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine full-time professional editors for operational continuity with part-time academic editors for subject expertise; provide renewable contracts and modest compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board as occasional advisers (not rubber stamps)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also an 'Editorial Board'... where people serve a 3 year term without pay, giving occasional advice to associate editors and lending their credibility to the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial boards as meaningful appeals/advisory bodies rather than merely honorific lists; ensure they contribute to journal standards and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate transparency and suitable target
rubrics_metrics.description: PRE receives about 3,500-4,000 submissions a year, of which about 55-60% get accepted... For comparison, PRL accepts roughly 20-25%... Nature accepts about 8%... In math journals true acceptance ratios are hard to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about acceptance rates; consider higher acceptance rates for community service journals (public-good argument) rather than using low rates solely to signal prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create highlighted selections (Editors' Suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer papers, PRE started making 'Editors' Suggestions'... a small number of articles the editors chose to highlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide curated highlights to reward and increase visibility of notable papers; such selections can be listed on CVs as minor awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee recognition program
rubrics_metrics.description: The APS instituted an outstanding referee award... to encourage quick and thorough refereeing. Each year, about 150 awardees across all APS journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a refereeing award program with nominations from Associate Editors and selection at editorial meetings to recognize and incentivize high-quality reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey/perspective article program
rubrics_metrics.description: At PRE, the editors occasionally solicit 'perspectives'... forward looking articles suggesting important questions and directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit shorter forward-looking pieces or perspectives to guide the field and provide venues for idea-setting articles beyond full surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: ArXiv integration and encouragement of preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: The APS is aware of the role the arXiv plays... So it encourages submissions consisting of arXiv numbers and subject areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design submission and editorial workflows that accept and integrate arXiv postings (arXiv overlay concepts) to reduce friction and embrace community dissemination norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate correctness verification from novelty/importance evaluation (mega journal idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mega journal would only check validity and 'publish' only based on correctness. When correctness is disentangled from evaluating novelty and importance, the point of the mega journal would be to help the authors get their proofs right and the papers accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a large community-run venue focused solely on technical correctness (possibly multiple 'baby megas') while traditional journals compete to select the most novel or important work, reducing redundant review for correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow journals to bid / compete for best papers (overlay linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The remnants of the existing general journals would... place bids on the best papers attracting them 'modulo publication in the mega journal'... the paper will be linked to the journal website in the 'arXiv overlay' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate publication (verification) from editorial selection/branding so journals can 'award' or 'host' papers while the canonical version is on arXiv; this fosters competition without redundant peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference-style competitive selection using arXiv preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: One can imagine a competitive conference system in the style of CS theory conferences... The conference submission could require a prior arXiv posting and later keep track of 'verified' papers (accepted to the mega journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conference-like deadlines and selection for rapid dissemination and community attention, tied to prior arXiv posting and subsequent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-boycott as consumer strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Boycott all non-free journals as a consumer! Do NOT download papers from journal websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a tactic to pressure publishers, encourage widespread use of free copies (arXiv, personal sites) and reduce reliance on paywalled downloads to weaken publishers' bargaining power with libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should post all papers freely online
rubrics_metrics.description: On your side as an author, make every(!) paper you ever wrote freely accessible. Put them on the arXiv, viXra, your own website, or anywhere you like as long as the search engines can find them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should proactively make all their work discoverable and accessible to reduce dependence on paywalled journals; if unsure how, ask for help — it's feasible for most mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers should prefer free copies (search strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reading papers... google it first. Google Scholar usually gives you multiple options on the download location. Choose the one in the arXiv or author’s website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use search engines to locate free versions before resorting to publisher sites; avoid clicking MathSciNet article links that go directly to paywalled pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: If paper unavailable, email author and request a copy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is recent but inaccessible for free. Then email to the authors and request the file of paper. Shame them into putting the paper online while you are at it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct author contact as a simple step to obtain and encourage public posting; many authors will respond promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: If necessary, repost paywalled papers for community access
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose now the paper is inaccessible for free, but the authors are non-responsive... Well, ok — download it from the journal website then via your library. But then be a mensch. Post the paper online. Yes, in violation of copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author endorses (controversially) reposting copyrighted copies to increase access if authors/publishers won't; this is framed as civil disobedience to weaken paywall dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course websites should link to free versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally, suppose you create a course website. Make sure all or at least most of your links are to free version of the articles. Download them all and repost them on your course website so the students can bypass the library redirect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should prioritize linking to freely available copies or repost them on course pages to reduce student reliance on library paywalls and normalize free access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct journal studies and appoint leadership for innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The AMS Council can sure use a 'Chair of journal innovation' whose job would be to conduct journal studies (like the many APS studies I mentioned above), or at least read other publishers’ studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society leadership should commission and act on systematic studies of editorial practices, acceptance, and production models to guide reform; create accountable roles for journal innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metrics and openness to shame/paywall pressure strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Every time you download an article... it gives publishers leverage to claim they are indispensable. Make download patterns show decreasing reliance and use that to pressure subscriptions/pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and use usage data strategically (e.g., librarians observing falling downloads of paywalled content) to negotiate lower prices or cancel subscriptions; public shaming and behavioral change can shift incentives.
